Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-2-prompt-long-0155", "row_sha256": "662ec67c04276fab50042fbef941109d74a7099d693d2037cdc842129b5cbdd2", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you put together an update about the rehearsal recording archive at Eastbank Repertory, for the people working with the collection, not a public announcement. It needs to read as a self-contained ordinary update, around 600 to 800 words, and have a clear final section. I have the details below in the order I remembered them, which isn't necessarily the order they should appear in. Please use all the relevant ones, and don't make it sound as if the inventory has settled every question. This is about the current work, not a pitch for the archive or a general history of the theater.

The collection is called the Back Room collection. Eastbank Repertory has kept rehearsal sound recordings from its studio and touring room, with dates running from 1991 through 2008. The first inventory covered 37 boxes. The labels and the finding ledger name nine productions, among them Harbor Lights, The Glass Orchard, and Weather Station. There are 214 carriers listed so far: 126 compact cassettes, 48 MiniDiscs, 22 DAT tapes, and 18 CDs. That total is from the inventory of the carriers encountered so far, not a claim about how many the theater ever made. Some box labels have production dates, some have only a title or a performer’s name, and there are gaps in the dates. Keep that difference between what the labels say and what we can identify from them.

There are five cartons that haven't been opened yet, and the ledger also lists 11 DAT tapes that the team hasn't located. It might be tempting to call the tapes missing, but we don't know that, and the cartons could change what can be accounted for. We do know the ledger entry is there; don't leave it out just because it has not been checked against a physical carrier. Don't imply the 11 are included in the 214, either, because the current count is only for carriers encountered. The next update should make those limits easy to follow without turning them into a dramatic mystery. The point is that the first inventory gives us useful locations and formats but isn't a complete reconciliation.

A small digitization pilot has worked with 12 cassettes and four DAT tapes, selected from the material already found. Together those sources produced about 19 hours of listening files. Ten files have had their waveform checks completed; the other six are still waiting for that check. The work used a playback-only deck. No one has baked, repaired, or otherwise treated any tape, so don't say that the physical recordings have been restored or that all the audio is ready for use. The files are working copies for review, not a public release. The pilot is limited to those 16 carriers, not all 214 and certainly not material in unopened cartons.

One of the people doing the listening, audio technician Mara Ellison, said, “You can hear the rehearsal room settle down after the first run-through.” Please include that as an ordinary reported quote, with her name and role, not as a slogan or a claim about every recording. It came from listening to the pilot material, and it should sit near the description of what the recordings let the team hear. The source tapes include spoken rehearsal discussion as well as run-throughs, so don't describe them as finished performances. The update can mention that the files make it easier to compare sound and sequence within the sampled sessions, but it shouldn't claim that a production history has been verified from them.

There is also a paperwork point that needs to stay separate from the technical work. Clearance forms are on file for four of the nine productions named in the ledger. Forms for the other five have not been reviewed. That is not the same as saying permission has been denied, and it is not a reason to describe the files as cleared for circulation. For now, access to the working files remains staff-only while the forms are reviewed. One recording includes people saying personal phone numbers aloud; that item needs a closer access review before anyone considers wider listening. Don't invent a decision about whether those numbers will be removed, or suggest that the review is finished.

Maybe use a numbered section for the practical status, if it fits naturally, but don't force a list where paragraphs read better. There are several related threads and the update should connect them: the inventory is one, the limited pilot is another, and access review is a third. Please don't collapse those into one claim that the archive is digitized or ready. Include the carrier counts and the formats accurately, and explain the relationship between the 16 pilot sources and the larger set. The names of the three productions above are examples from the nine, not a complete list; don't supply six more names. Keep the archive's scope at Eastbank Repertory and its rehearsal recordings.

For the ending, the full assessment we have at this point is that the current inventory can support questions about carrier locations and formats, but it cannot verify the complete production record or establish that the collection is complete. Comparing the inventory against the full holdings still depends on opening the five cartons and locating or accounting for the 11 DAT tapes listed in the ledger. Keep both conditions and that limited scope in the assessment. Don't turn it into a general verdict on the archive, and don't append a summary that makes it sound as though those checks have happened.

The next workroom visit is scheduled for 14 October. Two staff members are due to compare the carton labels with the ledger, and no further transfer is planned for that visit. That schedule is a separate practical detail for the final paragraph; don't imply the visit has already happened, or that it will resolve the discrepancy. Use connected, substantive paragraphs, an ordinary quote, and a clearly marked final section if useful. Please end on the visit information rather than a new recommendation or a made-up conclusion.", "output": "Write a self-contained, 600–800-word update for people working with Eastbank Repertory’s Back Room rehearsal recording archive. This is an ordinary internal update about current work, not a public announcement, a pitch, or a general history of the theater. Organize the information below into connected, substantive paragraphs and give the update a clear final section. A numbered section may be used for practical status if it fits naturally. Do not suggest that the inventory has settled every question.

**Collection and inventory**

Eastbank Repertory has kept rehearsal sound recordings from its studio and touring room, dated from 1991 through 2008. The first inventory covered 37 boxes and lists nine productions, including *Harbor Lights*, *The Glass Orchard*, and *Weather Station*. It records 214 carriers encountered so far: 126 compact cassettes, 48 MiniDiscs, 22 DAT tapes, and 18 CDs. Make clear that this is the count of carriers encountered in the inventory, not a count of everything the theater ever made. Some labels give production dates, while others give only a title or performer’s name; dates are incomplete. Distinguish what the labels say from what can be identified from them. The three named productions are examples, not a complete list; do not supply other production names.

Five cartons remain unopened. The finding ledger also lists 11 DAT tapes that the team has not located. The tapes are not known to be missing, and the unopened cartons could affect what can be accounted for. The ledger entry is real, but the 11 tapes are not included in the count of 214 carriers encountered so far. Explain that the first inventory provides useful information about locations and formats but is not a complete reconciliation. Do not make the discrepancy sound mysterious or imply that the checks have been completed.

**Digitization and listening**

A limited digitization pilot used 12 cassettes and four DAT tapes selected from material already found. Those 16 carriers produced about 19 hours of listening files. Waveform checks are complete for ten files; the other six are waiting for checks. The work used a playback-only deck. No tape has been baked, repaired, or otherwise treated. Describe the files as working copies for review, not as a public release, and do not say that the recordings have been restored or that all audio is ready for use. The pilot covers only those 16 carriers, not all 214 or anything in the unopened cartons.

Audio technician Mara Ellison said, “You can hear the rehearsal room settle down after the first run-through.” Include this as an ordinary reported quote, with her name and role, near the description of what the recordings let the team hear. It reflects listening to pilot material, not every recording, and should not be used as a slogan. The sources contain spoken rehearsal discussion as well as run-throughs, not just finished performances. The files make it easier to compare sound and sequence within the sampled sessions, but they do not verify a production history.

**Access and paperwork**

Clearance forms are on file for four of the nine productions named in the ledger; forms for the other five have not been reviewed. Do not describe this as a denial of permission or as clearance for circulation. Access to working files remains staff-only while the forms are reviewed. One recording includes people saying personal phone numbers aloud and needs closer access review before wider listening is considered. Do not invent a decision about removing the numbers or imply that the review is finished. Keep the inventory, limited digitization pilot, and access review distinct; do not describe the archive as digitized or ready.

**Assessment and next visit**

Include this full assessment, preserving its scope and conditions: the current inventory can support questions about carrier locations and formats, but it cannot verify the complete production record or establish that the collection is complete. Comparing the inventory against the full holdings still depends on opening the five cartons and locating or accounting for the 11 DAT tapes listed in the ledger. Do not turn this into a general verdict on the archive or append a summary suggesting those checks have happened.

End with the separate practical detail that the next workroom visit is scheduled for 14 October. Two staff members are due to compare the carton labels with the ledger, and no further transfer is planned for that visit. Do not imply that the visit has already happened or will resolve the discrepancy. End on this visit information, without adding a recommendation or conclusion."}]
